questions.q: In the forecasting model Sales_t = b0 + b1 x AdSpend_t, built for a Bengaluru apparel retailer, what role does Sales_t play?
options: It is the dependent (target) variable being forecast
It is an independent (predictor) variable driving the forecast
It is a lag feature carrying last period's value
It is the residual left over after fitting
questions.answer: It is the dependent (target) variable being forecast
questions.explanation: Sales is what the model predicts, so it is the dependent variable; AdSpend is the predictor. Students sometimes mix these up because both appear in the equation.

questions.q: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimates the coefficients of a linear regression by minimising which quantity?
options: The sum of the raw residuals
The sum of absolute residuals
The count of wrong predictions
The sum of squared residuals
questions.answer: The sum of squared residuals
questions.explanation: OLS picks the line that makes the sum of squared differences between actual and fitted values as small as possible. The plain sum of residuals is not used because positive and negative errors cancel out.

questions.q: In a regression forecast, what is a residual?
options: Predicted value minus the mean of the data
Actual value minus the mean of the data
Actual value minus the predicted value
The gap between the slope and the intercept
questions.answer: Actual value minus the predicted value
questions.explanation: A residual is the error of the model for one observation: actual minus fitted. Actual minus mean is the total deviation used in R-squared, not the residual.

questions.q: A demand planner adds 'sales_lag_1' as a feature in a regression model of weekly FMCG sales. What does this feature contain?
options: Next week's sales, shifted back one row so the model can learn from them
The previous week's sales, used as an input to predict this week's sales
The average weekly sales across the full history, repeated in every row
This week's sales after the seasonal component has been removed
questions.answer: The previous week's sales, used as an input to predict this week's sales
questions.explanation: A lag-1 feature shifts the series by one period so the model can use the last known value to predict the current one. Using next week's value would be the target, not a feature.

questions.q: What does the R-squared of a linear regression measure?
options: The percentage of forecasts that turn out exactly correct
The share of variation in the target explained by the model
The average size of the forecast error, in percentage terms
The slope of the fitted line expressed as a proportion
questions.answer: The share of variation in the target explained by the model
questions.explanation: R-squared is explained variation divided by total variation. It is not an accuracy percentage; error size is measured by MAE or RMSE.

questions.q: When splitting monthly sales data into training and test sets for a regression forecasting model, what is the correct approach?
options: Train on the earlier months and test on the later months, without shuffling
Randomly shuffle all months first and then hold out 20% of them as the test set
Test on the earliest months and train on the most recent months
Use every month for both training and testing to maximise the data
questions.answer: Train on the earlier months and test on the later months, without shuffling
questions.explanation: Forecasting means predicting the future from the past, so the test set must come after the training period. Random shuffling lets the model learn from future months, which inflates accuracy.

questions.q: In a linear regression Sales = b0 + b1 x Price + b2 x Promo, what does the intercept b0 represent?
options: The average change in sales per rupee of price
The error term that the model cannot explain
The maximum sales value the model can predict
Predicted sales when all predictors equal zero
questions.answer: Predicted sales when all predictors equal zero
questions.explanation: The intercept is the fitted value of the target when every X is zero. The change per unit of a predictor is a slope coefficient, not the intercept.

questions.q: What does multicollinearity mean in a multiple regression model?
options: The target is very strongly correlated with one of the predictors
The residuals of the model are correlated with each other over time
Two or more predictors are highly correlated with each other
The model is forecasting more than one dependent variable at once
questions.answer: Two or more predictors are highly correlated with each other
questions.explanation: Multicollinearity is correlation among the predictors themselves, which makes individual coefficients unstable. Correlation between residuals over time is autocorrelation, a different issue.

questions.q: Which scikit-learn class is used to fit an ordinary linear regression model in Python?
options: KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.neighbors
DecisionTreeRegressor from sklearn.tree
LinearRegression from sklearn.linear_model
RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.ensemble
questions.answer: LinearRegression from sklearn.linear_model
questions.explanation: LinearRegression in sklearn.linear_model fits OLS regression. The other classes fit KNN, tree and forest models.

questions.q: Why would an analyst add 0/1 dummy variables such as 'Diwali_month' or 'Q4' to a regression forecasting model?
options: To remove the long-term upward trend from the sales data
To capture the effect of festivals or seasons on sales
To rescale every predictor to the same 0-1 range
To increase the number of observations available
questions.answer: To capture the effect of festivals or seasons on sales
questions.explanation: Dummy variables convert categories such as festive months into numbers so the regression can estimate their effect. They do not detrend or rescale the data.

questions.q: A retailer's model is Sales (Rs lakh) = 120 + 4.5 x AdSpend (Rs lakh). How should the coefficient 4.5 be interpreted?
options: Each extra Rs 1 lakh of ad spend is linked to Rs 4.5 lakh higher forecast sales
Forecast sales will be Rs 4.5 lakh in any month in which ad spend is zero
Ad spend explains 4.5% of the month-to-month variation in sales
Each extra Rs 4.5 lakh of ad spend raises forecast sales by Rs 1 lakh
questions.answer: Each extra Rs 1 lakh of ad spend is linked to Rs 4.5 lakh higher forecast sales
questions.explanation: The slope is the change in the target for a one-unit change in the predictor. Sales at zero ad spend is the intercept (120), not the slope.

questions.q: A cafe chain forecasts daily cold-beverage sales with Sales_t = 50 + 2.0 x Temp_t + 0.8 x Sales_(t-1). Tomorrow's forecast temperature is 30 degrees and today's sales were 200 units. What is tomorrow's forecast?
options: 210 units
250 units
110 units
270 units
questions.answer: 270 units
questions.explanation: 50 + 2.0 x 30 + 0.8 x 200 = 50 + 60 + 160 = 270. 210 forgets the temperature term and 110 forgets the lag term.

questions.q: A monthly demand model for a Pune two-wheeler dealer has R-squared = 0.82. What is the correct interpretation?
options: 82% of the monthly forecasts will match actual demand exactly
The forecasts are off by about 18% on average each month
Monthly demand rises by 0.82 units for each one-unit rise in the predictors
82% of the variation in monthly demand is explained by the predictors
questions.answer: 82% of the variation in monthly demand is explained by the predictors
questions.explanation: R-squared is the share of variance explained, not a hit rate or an error percentage. Average percentage error would come from MAPE.

questions.q: A hotel's regression model predicted 500 room-nights for a weekend, but the actual was 540. What is the residual and what does it say?
options: -40; the model under-forecast demand
+40; the model over-forecast demand
+40; the model under-forecast demand
-40; the model over-forecast demand
questions.answer: +40; the model under-forecast demand
questions.explanation: Residual = actual - predicted = 540 - 500 = +40, so the forecast was too low. Computing predicted minus actual gives -40, a common sign error.

questions.q: In a regression of weekly bank branch footfall, the coefficient on 'number_of_public_holidays' has a p-value of 0.30. What is the best interpretation at the 5% level?
options: It explains about 30% of the variation in weekly footfall
Not statistically significant; a candidate for removal
Highly significant, since 0.30 is well above zero
Each extra holiday adds 0.30 visitors to footfall
questions.answer: Not statistically significant; a candidate for removal
questions.explanation: A p-value of 0.30 is far above 0.05, so we cannot reject that the true coefficient is zero. The p-value is not a share of variance or the coefficient value.

questions.q: Adding five new predictors to a sales model raised R-squared from 0.70 to 0.71, but adjusted R-squared fell from 0.69 to 0.66. What should the analyst conclude?
options: The new predictors add little real explanatory power, so keep the simpler model
The new model is better, because a higher R-squared always means better forecasts
All five new predictors must be significant, since R-squared went up after adding them
Adjusted R-squared is unreliable with many predictors, so it should be ignored here
questions.answer: The new predictors add little real explanatory power, so keep the simpler model
questions.explanation: R-squared never falls when predictors are added, so its small rise means little. Adjusted R-squared penalises extra predictors, and its drop signals they are not worth keeping.

questions.q: A plot of a regression model's residuals against time shows long runs of positive errors followed by long runs of negative errors. What does this suggest?
options: Residuals are autocorrelated, so lags or seasonality are missing
The model is fine, because the residuals still average out to zero
The predictors are multicollinear and one should be dropped
The rows should be shuffled before the model is refitted
questions.answer: Residuals are autocorrelated, so lags or seasonality are missing
questions.explanation: Runs of same-sign residuals mean errors are correlated over time, so the model has not captured some time pattern. Adding lag or seasonal terms is the usual fix; shuffling would only hide the issue.

questions.q: In a monthly sales model for a sweets manufacturer, the dummy 'Festive_month' (1 for Diwali and Dussehra months, 0 otherwise) has a coefficient of 35 (thousand kg). What does this mean?
options: Festive months account for about 35% of the manufacturer's total annual sales volume
Sales grow by about 35 thousand kg every month, starting from the festive season
The festive months have 35 thousand kg lower sales than other months, others constant
Festive months are forecast about 35 thousand kg higher than other months, others constant
questions.answer: Festive months are forecast about 35 thousand kg higher than other months, others constant
questions.explanation: A dummy coefficient is the average difference in the target between the category coded 1 and the base category. It is a level shift, not a growth rate or a share.

questions.q: A linear trend model for monthly e-commerce orders is Orders = 200 + 12t, where t = 1 is January 2024. What is the forecast for January 2026 (t = 25)?
options: 512 orders
488 orders
500 orders
212 orders
questions.answer: 500 orders
questions.explanation: 200 + 12 x 25 = 500. 512 uses t = 26 and 488 uses t = 24, both off-by-one errors in counting months.

questions.q: On a 4-week test period, a regression model's errors (actual - forecast) are 4, -2, -4 and 2 units. What is the RMSE?
options: 10.00 units
3.16 units
3.00 units
0.00 units
questions.answer: 3.16 units
questions.explanation: Squared errors 16, 4, 16, 4 average to 10 (the MSE), and RMSE = square root of 10 = 3.16. 3 is the MAE and 0 is the mean error, where positive and negative errors cancel.

questions.q: An analyst builds lag features on 5 years of daily sales, randomly shuffles all rows, and gets a test R-squared of 0.97. When used for next quarter's forecasts, accuracy drops sharply. What is the most likely reason?
options: An R-squared of 0.97 shows the model is too simple and is underfitting the sales data
Shuffling let the model train on days around each test day, leaking future information
Lag features should never be used inside a regression model for daily sales data
The test set was too large, so the model had too little data left for training
questions.answer: Shuffling let the model train on days around each test day, leaking future information
questions.explanation: With shuffling, the test days have neighbours from both before and after them in the training set, so the evaluation looks far better than true forecasting. A time-ordered split avoids this leakage.

questions.q: A supermarket wants to forecast tomorrow's sales today. An analyst uses 'same-day store footfall' as a predictor and gets an excellent fit. What is the problem?
options: Same-day footfall is unknown when forecasting, so it leaks; use lagged footfall
Footfall is a categorical variable, so regression cannot use it as a predictor
The model will underfit, because footfall is only weakly related to sales
There is no problem, since a better fit always means better live forecasts
questions.answer: Same-day footfall is unknown when forecasting, so it leaks; use lagged footfall
questions.explanation: A predictor must be available at forecast time. Tomorrow's footfall is only observed tomorrow, so the model cannot be used in practice; lagged or planned values are valid substitutes.

questions.q: A model is Sales_t = 30 + 0.6 x Sales_(t-1). Last month's actual sales were 100. Using the model recursively, what is the forecast two months ahead?
questions.explanation: Month 1: 30 + 0.6 x 100 = 90. Month 2: 30 + 0.6 x 90 = 84. 90 stops after one step, and 66 (30 + 0.36 x 100) forgets that the intercept also feeds through the first step.

questions.q: Online sales of a D2C brand have grown steadily every year and next year is expected to exceed anything seen so far. Why might a linear regression with a time trend be preferred over a single decision tree here?
options: Decision trees cannot accept a time index or any date-based feature as an input
Linear regression always produces lower test error than any decision tree model
Regression can extend the trend beyond past levels; a tree is capped at training levels
Decision trees need the data to be shuffled before training, losing the trend
questions.answer: Regression can extend the trend beyond past levels; a tree is capped at training levels
questions.explanation: A tree predicts leaf averages, so it can never forecast above the highest training level. A trend term in regression keeps extending the line, which suits a steadily growing series.

questions.q: For quarterly sales planning, a regression model with promotion spend has test MAPE 8.0% and Holt-Winters has test MAPE 7.5%. The marketing head must decide how much promotion budget to allocate. Which choice is most sensible?
options: Use Holt-Winters, because the model with the lower MAPE should always win
Use the regression, because it shows a higher R-squared on the training quarters
Use the regression, as it quantifies promotion effects at nearly equal accuracy
Reject both models and re-test them using a random train-test split instead
questions.answer: Use the regression, as it quantifies promotion effects at nearly equal accuracy
questions.explanation: The accuracy difference is small, and only the regression can answer 'what if we spend more on promotion'. Choosing purely on 0.5 percentage points of MAPE ignores the decision the forecast must support.

questions.q: A model is ln(Sales) = 2 + 0.05 x Discount_pct. What is the approximate effect of increasing the discount by 1 percentage point?
options: Sales rise by 0.05 units
Sales rise by about 5%
Sales rise by about 5 units
Sales rise by about 2%
questions.answer: Sales rise by about 5%
questions.explanation: With a log target, a coefficient b means roughly a 100 x b percent change in the target per unit change in X. Reading 0.05 as units ignores the log transformation.

questions.q: In a sales model, TV ad spend and digital ad spend have a correlation of 0.95 and VIFs above 10. The digital coefficient comes out negative, though managers are sure digital ads help sales. What is the best explanation?
options: Multicollinearity makes the separate coefficients unstable and unreliable
Digital ads genuinely reduce sales, so the budget should be cut
The model is underfitting and simply needs many more predictors
The negative sign proves that the sales data contains entry errors
questions.answer: Multicollinearity makes the separate coefficients unstable and unreliable
questions.explanation: When predictors move together, OLS cannot separate their effects and coefficient signs can flip. Combining the two spends or dropping one gives more stable interpretation.

questions.q: A regression with n = 50 observations and k = 4 predictors has R-squared = 0.80. What is the adjusted R-squared, using 1 - (1 - R2)(n - 1)/(n - k - 1)?
questions.explanation: 1 - 0.20 x 49/45 = 1 - 0.218 = 0.78. Adjusted R-squared is always at or below R-squared, so 0.82 is impossible and 0.20 is just 1 - R-squared.

questions.q: A residual plot for a chain's store-level sales model shows errors that fan out, becoming much larger for high-sales stores. What is the issue and a common remedy?
options: Multicollinearity; drop a predictor
Autocorrelation; shuffle the rows
Underfitting; add squared terms
Heteroscedasticity; model log of sales
questions.answer: Heteroscedasticity; model log of sales
questions.explanation: Error variance that grows with the level of the target is heteroscedasticity. A log transform turns absolute errors into roughly percentage errors and stabilises the variance.

questions.q: An analyst wants to choose how many lags (1 to 12) to include in a regression forecast of monthly sales. Which validation approach is most appropriate?
options: Standard shuffled 5-fold cross-validation across all of the months
Pick the number of lags that gives the highest training R-squared
Walk-forward validation, testing each fold on months after its training data
Validate on the first year and train on all of the later years
questions.answer: Walk-forward validation, testing each fold on months after its training data
questions.explanation: Walk-forward (rolling-origin) validation such as TimeSeriesSplit respects time order, mimicking how the model will actually forecast. Shuffled K-fold leaks future data and training R-squared always favours more lags.

references: Linear regression is a method that explains and forecasts a numeric outcome, such as monthly sales, as a straight-line combination of drivers like price, promotion spend, a time trend, seasonal dummies or last month's sales (lag features). The model estimates a coefficient for each driver using least squares, which minimises the squared gaps between actual and fitted values. Each coefficient tells us how much sales change for a one-unit change in that driver, holding others constant. We judge the model with R-squared on training data, but more importantly with RMSE or MAPE on a later, time-ordered test period, never a shuffled one.

Suppose our FMCG brand wants to forecast next month's sales. Linear regression would fit something like Sales = 120 + 4.5 x AdSpend + 0.6 x LastMonthSales + 35 x FestiveMonth. So every extra lakh on ads adds about 4.5 lakh of sales, festive months add 35, and last month's sales carry momentum. We fit it on past months, check it on the most recent months it has not seen, and look at residuals for leftover patterns. Its strength is that it can extend a trend into the future, which tree models cannot, but it assumes relationships are linear and gets shaky when drivers like TV and digital spend are highly correlated.

As a manager, I would use linear regression when I need a forecast that also explains why: how much price, promotions or festivals move demand. It is fast, transparent and can extrapolate a growth trend. The cautions are that it only captures straight-line effects unless we add transformations, correlated drivers make individual coefficients unreliable, and every input must be known at forecast time, so we use lagged values rather than same-day figures to avoid leakage. I would trust it only after testing on a later hold-out period and comparing its RMSE or MAPE with simple benchmarks like Holt-Winters or a naive forecast.

questions.q: In a regression decision tree forecasting daily sales, what value does a leaf node predict?
options: The average sales of the training rows in that leaf
The maximum sales among the training rows in that leaf
The sales of the most recent day in the training data
A straight-line trend fitted to the rows inside the leaf
questions.answer: The average sales of the training rows in that leaf
questions.explanation: A regression tree's leaf output is the mean of the training targets that fall into it. It does not fit a line or take the maximum.

questions.q: What is the root node of a decision tree?
options: The bottom node of a branch, where the final prediction is read off
The node that ends up holding the fewest training observations
The feature with the lowest importance, placed first by convention
The top node holding all training data, where the first split is made
questions.answer: The top node holding all training data, where the first split is made
questions.explanation: The tree starts at the root with all data and splits downward; prediction nodes at the bottom are leaves. Confusing root with leaf is a common slip.

questions.q: By default, which criterion does scikit-learn's DecisionTreeRegressor use to choose splits?
options: Reduction in Gini impurity
Reduction in entropy
Reduction in squared error
Increase in adjusted R-squared
questions.answer: Reduction in squared error
questions.explanation: Regression trees choose the split that most reduces the squared error (variance) within the child nodes. Gini and entropy are for classification trees.

questions.q: A classification tree predicts whether next week's demand at a store will be 'High' or 'Low'. Which measure is commonly used to choose its splits?
options: Mean squared error
Gini impurity
Root mean squared error
MAPE
questions.answer: Gini impurity
questions.explanation: Classification trees use Gini impurity or entropy to measure how mixed the classes are in a node. Squared-error measures are used for regression trees.

questions.q: What does the max_depth hyperparameter control in a decision tree?
options: The number of separate trees that are built and then averaged
The maximum number of levels of splits, which limits complexity
The number of input features the tree is allowed to look at
The smallest value that any leaf prediction is allowed to take
questions.answer: The maximum number of levels of splits, which limits complexity
questions.explanation: max_depth caps how many successive splits a path can have, which controls overfitting. The number of trees is a forest or boosting setting.

questions.q: What typically happens when a decision tree is grown very deep with no limits?
options: It memorises training noise and forecasts poorly on new periods
It underfits and ends up predicting the same value for every period
It becomes mathematically identical to a linear regression model
It automatically improves accuracy on the later test periods as well
questions.answer: It memorises training noise and forecasts poorly on new periods
questions.explanation: A fully grown tree can place almost every observation in its own leaf, fitting noise. Training error falls but error on later periods rises.

questions.q: Do decision trees require features such as price (in rupees) and temperature (in degrees) to be scaled to the same range?
options: Yes, otherwise the large-valued features dominate the splits
Yes, because every tree input must lie between 0 and 1
Only when the target being predicted is a category label
No, because each split is a threshold on a single feature
questions.answer: No, because each split is a threshold on a single feature
questions.explanation: Trees compare one feature against a threshold, so the units do not matter. Scaling is essential for distance-based methods like KNN, not trees.

questions.q: What is pruning in decision trees?
options: Adding extra branches so that training error falls further
Removing outlier rows from the training data before fitting
Cutting back branches that add little predictive value
Dropping the least important feature before the tree is grown
questions.answer: Cutting back branches that add little predictive value
questions.explanation: Pruning cuts back splits that do not improve generalisation, giving a simpler tree. It operates on the tree, not on rows or columns of the data.

questions.q: If you plot a regression tree's forecast against a single input such as temperature, what shape does it take?
options: A single smooth straight line
A smooth curve with no jumps
A step function with flat segments
A random scatter of points
questions.answer: A step function with flat segments
questions.explanation: Each leaf gives one constant value, so predictions jump between flat levels at the split thresholds. A straight line is what linear regression produces.

questions.q: What does the min_samples_leaf hyperparameter set in a decision tree?
options: The minimum number of leaves the finished tree must have
The minimum number of training rows allowed in a leaf
The minimum number of levels the tree must grow to
The minimum number of features checked at each split
questions.answer: The minimum number of training rows allowed in a leaf
questions.explanation: min_samples_leaf stops splits that would leave very few observations in a leaf, which smooths predictions and reduces overfitting.

questions.q: A tree for daily store sales splits first on 'Promo = Yes?'. If Yes, it splits on 'Weekend?' (Yes: 820, No: 610). If No, it splits on 'lag_1 > 500?' (Yes: 540, No: 380). What is the forecast for a weekday with no promotion when yesterday's sales were 450?
questions.explanation: No promo leads to the lag_1 split; 450 is not above 500, so the forecast is 380. Choosing 610 wrongly follows the promo branch for weekdays.

questions.q: Using the same tree (Promo Yes -> Weekend? Yes 820 / No 610; Promo No -> lag_1 > 500? Yes 540 / No 380), what is the forecast for a Wednesday with a promotion running and yesterday's sales of 700?
questions.explanation: Promo = Yes goes to the Weekend split, and Wednesday is not a weekend, giving 610. The lag_1 value is irrelevant on the promo branch, so 540 is a misread.

questions.q: Five training days fall into one leaf of a regression tree, with sales of 100, 110, 120, 150 and 170 units. What does the leaf predict?
options: 120 units
170 units
650 units
130 units
questions.answer: 130 units
questions.explanation: The leaf predicts the mean: 650 / 5 = 130. 120 is the median and 650 is the total.

questions.q: A tree forecasting daily sales reports feature importances: lag_7 = 0.55, promo = 0.25, temperature = 0.15, day_of_week = 0.05. What is the best interpretation?
options: Forecast sales rise by 0.55 units for every one-unit rise in last week's same-day sales
lag_7 by itself accounts for exactly 55% of the sales level in every week of the data
lag_7 did the most to reduce prediction error, but this shows neither cause nor direction
day_of_week should be removed because its low score shows it is causing poor forecasts
questions.answer: lag_7 did the most to reduce prediction error, but this shows neither cause nor direction
questions.explanation: Impurity-based importance measures each feature's share of total error reduction in the tree. It is not a coefficient and says nothing about direction or cause.

questions.q: A decision tree has training RMSE of 2 units and test RMSE of 45 units on later months. What is the best next step?
options: Grow the tree deeper so that the test error comes down as well
Limit growth by reducing max_depth or raising min_samples_leaf
Shuffle all rows before splitting so the test error looks fairer
Fold the test months into training and report the training RMSE
questions.answer: Limit growth by reducing max_depth or raising min_samples_leaf
questions.explanation: A huge gap between training and test error is classic overfitting, so the tree must be constrained. Shuffling or reporting training error would only hide the problem.

questions.q: Ice-cream sales at a Chennai outlet stay flat until temperature crosses about 35 degrees, then jump sharply. Why can a decision tree capture this naturally?
options: Trees split on thresholds, so a jump at 35 degrees is learned directly
Trees fit a straight line through temperature, which bends at 35
Trees need temperature turned into a 0/1 dummy before they can use it
Trees average all observations together regardless of the temperature
questions.answer: Trees split on thresholds, so a jump at 35 degrees is learned directly
questions.explanation: A split such as 'Temp > 35' directly represents a threshold effect. Linear regression would need a manually created dummy or transformation to do the same.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of leaves in a binary decision tree with max_depth = 3?
questions.explanation: Each level can double the number of nodes: 2^3 = 8 leaves. 6 comes from adding 2 per level and 3 just repeats the depth.

questions.q: In a hotel's booking data, promotions lift bookings strongly on weekends but barely on weekdays. How does a decision tree handle this?
options: It cannot capture any interaction between two features at all
It needs an explicit Promo x Weekend column, as regression does
It averages the promo effect equally across all days of the week
It splits on Weekend, then on Promo, capturing the interaction
questions.answer: It splits on Weekend, then on Promo, capturing the interaction
questions.explanation: Successive splits on different features let a tree model effects that depend on each other. Linear regression needs an explicit interaction term for this.

questions.q: In a regression tree for monthly sales, the highest leaf value is Rs 85 lakh (the highest single training month was Rs 90 lakh). What is the largest forecast this tree can ever produce?
options: Rs 90 lakh
No upper limit
Rs 85 lakh
Rs 170 lakh
questions.answer: Rs 85 lakh
questions.explanation: Predictions are always one of the leaf means, so the maximum is the highest leaf mean, 85. A single month's value of 90 is averaged with others in its leaf.

questions.q: A weekly sales tree shows 'returns_count for the same week' with importance 0.90, far above all other features. What should the analyst suspect?
options: Returns are the true driver and the model is working very well
Leakage, since same-week returns are known only after the sales
The tree is underfitting and needs a much larger max_depth
The returns feature needs to be scaled before it is used
questions.answer: Leakage, since same-week returns are known only after the sales
questions.explanation: A single feature with overwhelming importance often signals leakage. Same-week returns are a consequence of sales and will not be available when forecasting.

questions.q: A parent node has weekly sales of 10, 20, 30 and 40 (MSE = 125). Splitting into {10, 20} and {30, 40} gives each child an MSE of 25. What is the reduction in weighted MSE from this split?
questions.explanation: Weighted child MSE = (2/4) x 25 + (2/4) x 25 = 25, so the reduction is 125 - 25 = 100. 125 is the parent MSE and 25 is the child MSE, not the reduction.

questions.q: An e-commerce firm's sales grow about 20% a year. A tree trained on 2021-2024 with a time index forecasts 2025 as a flat line at the 2024 level. What is the best fix?
options: Detrend first (model growth or residuals after a trend), then use the tree
Increase max_depth so that the leaves can reach higher sales values
Shuffle the training rows so 2025-like patterns appear in training
Add new leaves for 2025 by hand using the expected growth rate
questions.answer: Detrend first (model growth or residuals after a trend), then use the tree
questions.explanation: Trees can only output values seen in training, so a rising trend must be removed first and added back later. A deeper tree still cannot exceed the training range.

questions.q: Trees of depth 2, 4, 6, 8 and 12 have validation RMSE (on the latest months) of 60, 42, 38, 40 and 55, while training RMSE keeps falling. Which depth should be chosen?
questions.explanation: Depth 6 gives the lowest validation error; beyond it the tree overfits as validation error rises. Depth 12 has the lowest training error, which is the misleading choice.

questions.q: Adding just two weeks of new data completely changes a decision tree's first split and its forecasts. What does this illustrate, and what is the usual remedy?
options: High bias; switch to a shallower tree with fewer levels of splits
Bad new data; discard the two new weeks and keep the old tree
High variance; average many trees in an ensemble such as a random forest
A coding error; trees are unaffected by small changes in data
questions.answer: High variance; average many trees in an ensemble such as a random forest
questions.explanation: Small data changes can flip early splits and cascade through a tree, which is high variance. Averaging many trees reduces this instability.

questions.q: A node in a stock-out classification tree has 40 'Stock-out' and 60 'No stock-out' weeks. What is its Gini impurity?
questions.explanation: Gini = 1 - (0.4^2 + 0.6^2) = 1 - 0.52 = 0.48. 0.52 is the sum of squares, a step short, and 0.24 is 0.4 x 0.6 without the factor of 2.

questions.q: A retail operations head wants simple, explainable rules to plan store staffing. A depth-3 tree has MAPE 9% and a 500-tree random forest has MAPE 7.5%. Which is the most defensible choice?
options: The random forest, as the most accurate model always wins
The depth-3 tree, as managers can read and act on its rules
A fully grown tree, for both higher accuracy and simplicity
Neither, as tree models cannot be used to forecast staffing
questions.answer: The depth-3 tree, as managers can read and act on its rules
questions.explanation: The stated need is explainable rules, and a shallow tree delivers them with only a small accuracy loss. A fully grown tree is neither simple nor reliably accurate.

questions.q: For 100 days of sales, split A (Promo) gives children of 30 days with MSE 50 and 70 days with MSE 100. Split B (Weekend) gives two children of 50 days, each with MSE 80. Which split does a regression tree choose?
options: Split B, as its weighted MSE is 80 versus 85 for A
Split A, as it has one very pure child with MSE 50
Split A, as its weighted MSE is 75 versus 80 for B
Either, as both have the same weighted MSE of 80
questions.answer: Split B, as its weighted MSE is 80 versus 85 for A
questions.explanation: Split A: (30 x 50 + 70 x 100)/100 = 85; split B: 80. The tree picks the lower weighted error; 75 is the unweighted average of A's children, a common slip.

questions.q: A tree is trained on only 60 monthly observations with min_samples_leaf = 1 and no depth limit. Forecasts swing wildly from month to month. What is the best adjustment?
options: Lower min_samples_leaf to 0 so that every month gets its own leaf
Remove all lag features so the tree relies only on calendar data
Switch to a random train-test split to smooth the forecast errors
Raise min_samples_leaf (say to 5) so leaves average several months
questions.answer: Raise min_samples_leaf (say to 5) so leaves average several months
questions.explanation: With one observation per leaf the tree simply memorises months. Requiring more observations per leaf averages out noise and gives steadier forecasts.

questions.q: A tree forecasts weekly sales with one rule: if lag_1 > 300 predict 350, otherwise predict 250. Last week's actual sales were 280. Forecasting recursively, what are the forecasts for the next two weeks?
questions.explanation: Week 1: lag_1 = 280 is not above 300, so 250. Week 2 uses the forecast 250 as lag_1, again giving 250. Answering 350 assumes sales rise without any rule producing it.

questions.q: A node in a classification tree has 25% 'Stock-out' weeks and 75% 'No stock-out' weeks. What is its entropy (base 2), to 2 decimals?
questions.explanation: Entropy = -(0.25 x log2 0.25 + 0.75 x log2 0.75) = 0.50 + 0.31 = 0.81. 0.38 is the Gini impurity (1 - 0.0625 - 0.5625), and 1.00 is the entropy of a 50-50 node.

references: A decision tree forecasts by asking a series of yes/no questions about the inputs, like 'Is there a promotion?' or 'Were last week's sales above 500?', and following the branches down to a leaf. Each leaf's forecast is the average of past observations that ended up there. The tree chooses each split to reduce error as much as possible, using squared error for numbers or Gini for categories. Trees handle non-linear and threshold effects and interactions without scaling, but a deep tree overfits, and a tree can never forecast beyond the range of values it saw in training, so trends must be handled separately.

Think of a store manager's rule book for daily sales. If there is a promotion and it is a weekend, expect about 820 units; promotion on a weekday, about 610; no promotion but strong sales yesterday, about 540; otherwise about 380. A decision tree learns exactly such rules from historical data, using lag features like yesterday's sales and calendar features like weekend or festival. We control its size with max depth or minimum samples per leaf, otherwise it memorises noise. We test it on the most recent weeks, not shuffled data, and remember that its forecasts are flat steps capped at past levels.

I would use a decision tree when the business needs forecasts that are easy to explain, for example staffing rules for stores. Its splits show which drivers matter, it captures thresholds and interactions like promotions working mainly on weekends, and it needs little data preparation. The weaknesses are instability, since small data changes can reshape the tree, overfitting if it grows too deep, and no extrapolation of growth trends. So I would keep the tree shallow or pruned, validate it on a later time period, check feature importance for signs of leakage, and move to a random forest or boosting if accuracy matters more than readability.

questions.q: How does a KNN regression model produce a sales forecast for a new period?
options: It averages the target values of the k most similar past observations
It fits a straight line through all the data
It builds a sequence of yes/no splits
It copies the value of the most recent observation in the series directly
questions.answer: It averages the target values of the k most similar past observations
questions.explanation: KNN finds the k nearest neighbours in feature space and averages their targets. Fitting a line is linear regression and splits are decision trees.

questions.q: What does 'k' represent in the KNN model?
options: The number of lag and calendar features used in each data row
The number of lags in the series
The number of training periods
The number of nearest neighbours used to make a prediction
questions.answer: The number of nearest neighbours used to make a prediction
questions.explanation: k is how many neighbours are consulted. It is a tuning parameter, separate from the number of features or lags.

questions.q: Which distance measure is most commonly used by default to find neighbours in KNN?
options: Gini impurity
Correlation coefficient
Euclidean distance
Mean absolute percentage error
questions.answer: Euclidean distance
questions.explanation: Euclidean (straight-line) distance is the usual default. Gini is a tree split measure and MAPE is a forecast accuracy measure.

questions.q: Why is KNN called a 'lazy learner'?
options: It uses only a small sample of the data
It does not build a model during training; it stores the data and does the work at prediction time
It always predicts the mean of the target
It trains quickly because it ignores most features
questions.answer: It does not build a model during training; it stores the data and does the work at prediction time
questions.explanation: KNN simply memorises the training set and computes distances when a forecast is requested. That makes training instant but prediction slow on large datasets.

questions.q: Why must features usually be scaled before applying KNN?
options: Scaling makes the model linear
Distances are dominated by features with large numeric ranges unless all features are put on a similar scale
KNN cannot accept negative numbers
Scaling cuts the number of neighbours KNN needs to examine, so each prediction becomes much faster and more stable
questions.answer: Distances are dominated by features with large numeric ranges unless all features are put on a similar scale
questions.explanation: A feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in single digits when computing distance. Standardisation or min-max scaling gives each feature a fair say.

questions.q: What is the typical effect of using a very small k, such as k = 1?
options: Forecasts become noisy and the model tends to overfit
Forecasts become flat and the model underfits
Forecasts become very smooth and the model tends to underfit
Feature scaling is no longer needed
questions.answer: Forecasts become noisy and the model tends to overfit
questions.explanation: With k = 1 the forecast copies a single neighbour, including its noise, giving low bias but high variance. Very large k produces the flat, underfit behaviour.

questions.q: In KNN classification (for example, predicting 'High' or 'Low' demand), how is the class decided?
options: By averaging the neighbours' class labels as numbers
By choosing the class of the farthest neighbour
By choosing the class that is rarest in the data
By majority vote among the k nearest neighbours
questions.answer: By majority vote among the k nearest neighbours
questions.explanation: For classification, KNN assigns the most common class among the neighbours. Averaging is used for regression targets.

questions.q: Which scikit-learn class is used for KNN regression?
options: KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn.tree
LinearRegression from sklearn.linear_model
KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.neighbors
XGBRegressor from xgboost
questions.answer: KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.neighbors
questions.explanation: KNeighborsRegressor in sklearn.neighbors fits KNN for numeric targets; KNeighborsClassifier is the classification version and lives in sklearn.neighbors, not sklearn.tree.

questions.q: When KNN is used to forecast a time series using lag features, what are the 'neighbours'?
options: The calendar periods falling immediately before and after the forecast date in the history
Stores located geographically closest
Past periods whose recent sales pattern (lag values) looks most similar to the current one
The k largest sales values in history
questions.answer: Past periods whose recent sales pattern (lag values) looks most similar to the current one
questions.explanation: With lag features, each row describes a recent pattern, so KNN finds past moments that looked similar and uses what happened next. Physical nearness or calendar adjacency is not what is measured.

questions.q: What is the 'curse of dimensionality' in the context of KNN?
options: With many rows, KNN cannot store the data
With many features, distances become less meaningful and all points look similarly far apart
With many neighbours averaged together, forecasts become too noisy and unstable to rely on for any planning
With many periods, seasonality disappears
questions.answer: With many features, distances become less meaningful and all points look similarly far apart
questions.explanation: As dimensions grow, the gap between the nearest and farthest neighbours shrinks, so 'nearest' carries little information. Feature selection helps.

questions.q: For next week's demand at a Hyderabad outlet, KNN with k = 3 finds neighbours whose following-week sales were 200, 230 and 260 units. What is the forecast?
options: 230 units
200 units
260 units
690 units
questions.answer: 230 units
questions.explanation: The forecast is the mean: (200 + 230 + 260)/3 = 230. 690 is the sum, not the average.

questions.q: Two weeks are described by (lag_1, lag_2) = (120, 100) and (124, 103). What is the Euclidean distance between them?
questions.explanation: sqrt((124 - 120)^2 + (103 - 100)^2) = sqrt(16 + 9) = 5. 7 is the Manhattan distance and 25 forgets the square root.

questions.q: A KNN classifier with k = 5 predicts tomorrow's demand category. The neighbours are High, Low, High, High, Low. What is the prediction?
options: Low
A tie, so no prediction
Medium
High
questions.answer: High
questions.explanation: High has 3 votes against 2 for Low, so the majority is High. With an odd k and two classes there cannot be a tie.

questions.q: A KNN model for store sales uses store area (1,000 to 50,000 sq ft) and discount (0 to 30%) without scaling. What will happen?
options: Discount will dominate the distance, because percentage features are automatically weighted more by KNN
Both features will count equally
Store area will dominate the distance, so discount will barely affect which stores are neighbours
The model will fail to run
questions.answer: Store area will dominate the distance, so discount will barely affect which stores are neighbours
questions.explanation: Differences in area run into thousands while discount differences are at most 30, so unscaled distance is almost entirely driven by area.

questions.q: Discount ranges from 0% to 30% in the training data. What is the min-max scaled value of a 12% discount?
questions.explanation: (12 - 0)/(30 - 0) = 0.4. 0.12 just converts the percentage to a fraction without using the range.

questions.q: On the latest 3 months held out as a test set, KNN gives: k = 1 train RMSE 0, test RMSE 48; k = 7 train RMSE 20, test RMSE 30; k = 25 train RMSE 38, test RMSE 41. Which k should be chosen?
options: Any k, since they are equivalent
questions.explanation: k = 7 has the lowest test error. k = 1 has a perfect training fit but overfits, and k = 25 is too smooth and underfits.

questions.q: The highest weekly sales in a KNN model's training data is 900 units. Using plain KNN regression on sales levels, what is the highest forecast it can make?
options: 900 units
Unlimited, depending on the trend
1,800 units
The average of all weeks
questions.answer: 900 units
questions.explanation: A KNN forecast is an average of training targets, so it can never exceed the largest one. This is why KNN, like trees, cannot extrapolate a growth trend.

questions.q: A bank's KNN model for daily cash withdrawals trains in seconds but takes far too long to produce forecasts for 5,000 ATMs. Why?
options: KNN retrains its whole model from scratch for every single ATM forecast that is requested
The number of neighbours grows with the data
KNN fits a separate regression for each ATM
Each prediction requires computing distances to every stored training observation
questions.answer: Each prediction requires computing distances to every stored training observation
questions.explanation: KNN does its work at prediction time by scanning the training data for neighbours. Large training sets therefore make prediction slow, not training.

questions.q: To forecast next week's sales of a soft drink with KNN, which feature vector is most suitable for each row?
options: Next week's sales and the week after's
A random week number
Sales in each of the previous 4 weeks, plus a festival-week flag
The row number after shuffling the data
questions.answer: Sales in each of the previous 4 weeks, plus a festival-week flag
questions.explanation: Recent lags and known calendar flags describe the current situation and are available at forecast time. Future sales cannot be features, and shuffled row numbers carry no meaning.

questions.q: An analyst standardises (z-scores) all 5 years of data and then splits it into the first 4 years for training and the last year for testing. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since scaling does not affect KNN
The scaler saw the test year's mean and spread, leaking future data; fit it on training years only
Standardisation must be replaced by shuffling
Nothing is wrong, because scaling with all available years gives the most stable and accurate mean and spread
questions.answer: The scaler saw the test year's mean and spread, leaking future data; fit it on training years only
questions.explanation: Fitting the scaler on all data lets test-period statistics shape the training features. Fit on the training period, then apply the same transformation to the test period.

questions.q: A distance-weighted KNN (weight = 1/distance) has three neighbours at distances 1, 2 and 4 with next-week sales of 100, 160 and 200 units. What is the forecast (to 2 decimals)?
options: 153.33 units
131.43 units
230.00 units
100.00 units
questions.answer: 131.43 units
questions.explanation: Weights 1, 0.5, 0.25 give (100 + 80 + 50)/1.75 = 131.43. 153.33 is the unweighted mean and 230 forgets to divide by the sum of weights.

questions.q: Query week: (lag_1, lag_2) = (10, 8), already scaled. Training rows: A (9, 8) -> 50; B (12, 9) -> 60; C (10, 5) -> 40; D (15, 15) -> 90. Using Euclidean distance and k = 2, what is the forecast?
questions.explanation: Distances: A = 1, B = 2.24, C = 3, D = 8.60, so the nearest two are A and B, giving (50 + 60)/2 = 55. 45 wrongly picks C over B, and 50 is the k = 1 answer.

questions.q: A quick-commerce firm's order volumes grow every month. A KNN model on order levels keeps forecasting values near past peaks and under-forecasts. What is the best fix?
options: Increase k so that more neighbours are averaged, which lifts the forecasts toward recent peaks
Remove feature scaling
Use a random split to include future months in training
Model month-on-month changes or growth rates with KNN and convert back to levels
questions.answer: Model month-on-month changes or growth rates with KNN and convert back to levels
questions.explanation: Averages of past levels cannot exceed past levels, so a growing series must be differenced or expressed as growth first. A larger k only makes forecasts flatter.

questions.q: Query store: area 20,000 sq ft, discount 10%. Store P: 20,100 sq ft, 25%. Store Q: 21,000 sq ft, 10%. Area ranges 1,000-50,000 and discount 0-30. Which store is the nearest neighbour before and after min-max scaling?
options: Q before scaling, P after scaling
P both before and after scaling
P before scaling, Q after scaling
Q both before and after scaling
questions.answer: P before scaling, Q after scaling
questions.explanation: Unscaled: P is about 101 away and Q is 1,000 away, so P wins. Scaled: P = sqrt(0.002^2 + 0.5^2) is about 0.50 and Q is about 0.02, so Q wins because the discount difference now counts.

questions.q: An analyst adds 60 lag, rolling and calendar features to a KNN sales model, and test error gets worse than with 6 well-chosen lags. What is the most likely explanation?
options: KNN needs at least 100 features to work well
More features always reduce bias, so test error must be wrong
Too many features make distances less informative, so the 'nearest' neighbours are no longer truly similar
The model now extrapolates too aggressively
questions.answer: Too many features make distances less informative, so the 'nearest' neighbours are no longer truly similar
questions.explanation: This is the curse of dimensionality: irrelevant features add noise to every distance. KNN benefits from a small set of relevant, scaled features.

questions.q: An e-commerce app needs millions of real-time demand forecasts a day across 500 SKUs using 10 years of history. Why is KNN a poor choice?
options: KNN cannot handle more than one SKU at a time, so 500 separate models would have to be retrained every single day
Every forecast must search the full history for neighbours, making predictions slow and costly at scale
KNN models take days to train
KNN cannot use lag features
questions.answer: Every forecast must search the full history for neighbours, making predictions slow and costly at scale
questions.explanation: KNN's cost is at prediction time, which is the bottleneck for real-time serving. A trained model such as a tree ensemble or linear model predicts far faster.

questions.q: In a KNN model with 400 training weeks, what happens if k is set to 400?
options: Every forecast equals the overall average of the training weeks, so the model underfits
Every forecast equals the most recent week
The model overfits because it uses all the data
Forecasts become highly sensitive to recent changes, since every recent week now acts as a neighbour
questions.answer: Every forecast equals the overall average of the training weeks, so the model underfits
questions.explanation: When k equals the training size, all rows are neighbours, so every forecast is the same overall mean. This is extreme high bias, the opposite of k = 1.

questions.q: On a 12-week time-ordered test, KNN has MAE 52 units while a seasonal naive forecast (same week last year) has MAE 48 units. What should the manager conclude?
options: Adopt KNN because machine learning is more advanced
KNN is better because its MAE is higher
The benchmark is invalid because it uses no features
KNN adds no value over the simple benchmark, so use the seasonal naive or improve KNN's features before adopting it
questions.answer: KNN adds no value over the simple benchmark, so use the seasonal naive or improve KNN's features before adopting it
questions.explanation: A model must beat simple benchmarks to justify its complexity. Here the naive method is more accurate, so KNN should not replace it as is.

questions.q: A KNN classifier with k = 4 labels weeks as 'Promote' or 'Don't promote'. For one week the neighbours split 2-2. What is the standard way to avoid this problem?
options: Keep k = 4 and break ties by picking a class at random each time
Use k = 2 so ties disappear
Remove feature scaling
Use an odd k (for example 3 or 5) for two-class problems
questions.answer: Use an odd k (for example 3 or 5) for two-class problems
questions.explanation: With two classes, an odd k guarantees a majority. k = 2 makes ties even more likely, not less.

questions.q: A sweets brand has only 3 Diwali weeks in its history. A KNN model with k = 10, using lags and a festival flag, is asked to forecast the coming Diwali week. What is the likely problem?
options: KNN will extrapolate above every past Diwali week because k is large
The festival flag forces all 10 neighbours to be Diwali weeks
At least 7 of the 10 neighbours must be ordinary weeks, pulling the Diwali forecast down
With k = 10 the model overfits to the single most similar Diwali week
questions.answer: At least 7 of the 10 neighbours must be ordinary weeks, pulling the Diwali forecast down
questions.explanation: Only 3 festival weeks exist, so at least 7 neighbours are normal weeks and their lower sales drag the average down. A smaller k, a stronger weight on the festival flag or a separate festival model helps.

references: K-nearest neighbours (KNN) forecasts by analogy. For a new period, it looks through history for the k most similar situations, measured by distance on features such as the last few weeks' sales, promotions or festival flags, and then averages what happened next in those situations. For classification it takes a majority vote. There is no real training step; the model just stores the data, which makes prediction slow on large datasets. Features must be scaled so that large-unit variables do not dominate distance, k is tuned on a later validation period, and because it averages past values it cannot forecast beyond levels seen before.

Imagine forecasting next week's sales for a mobile store. KNN asks: in the past, when were the last four weeks' sales most like these four weeks? Say it finds three such weeks, and the week after each sold 200, 230 and 260 units; the forecast is their average, 230. If k is 1, we copy one week and get noisy forecasts; if k is huge, everything becomes the overall average. We scale features like store size and discount first, choose k using the most recent months as a test set, and, since KNN cannot exceed past levels, we model growth or changes when sales are trending.

From a manager's view, KNN is a simple, intuitive method: 'find similar past situations and see what happened'. It needs no assumptions about linear relationships, so it can capture odd patterns. But it has practical limits: it is slow at prediction time for big data, sensitive to unscaled features and irrelevant variables, prone to overfitting with small k and underfitting with large k, and blind to trends because it only averages past outcomes. I would use it as one candidate model on a modest dataset with a few good lag features, and adopt it only if it beats simple benchmarks like seasonal naive on a time-ordered test.

questions.q: What is a random forest?
options: An ensemble of many decision trees, each built on random rows and features, with predictions combined
A single very deep decision tree
A linear regression with random coefficients
A sequence of decision trees built one after another, where each new tree corrects the previous tree's errors
questions.answer: An ensemble of many decision trees, each built on random rows and features, with predictions combined
questions.explanation: Random forests combine many randomised trees built independently. Building trees sequentially to correct errors describes boosting.

questions.q: What does 'bagging', the idea behind random forests, stand for?
options: Balanced aggregate gradient
Boosted averaging
Bias aggregation
Bootstrap aggregating
questions.answer: Bootstrap aggregating
questions.explanation: Bagging = bootstrap aggregating: train models on bootstrap samples and aggregate their predictions. Boosting is a different, sequential technique.

questions.q: What is a bootstrap sample in a random forest?
options: A sample of half the training rows drawn without replacement, so no row is repeated
The most recent 20% of the data
A sample of the same size as the training data drawn with replacement
A sample containing only the most important features
questions.answer: A sample of the same size as the training data drawn with replacement
questions.explanation: Drawing with replacement means some rows appear multiple times and others not at all, giving each tree a different view of the data.

questions.q: How does a random forest regressor produce its final sales forecast?
options: By taking the prediction of the best tree
By averaging the predictions of all its trees
By multiplying the trees' predictions
By taking the prediction of the last tree built
questions.answer: By averaging the predictions of all its trees
questions.explanation: Each tree votes with a number and the forest reports the mean. Picking one 'best' tree would lose the variance-reduction benefit.

questions.q: What does the max_features hyperparameter control in a random forest?
options: The total number of features kept in the data after feature selection
How many randomly chosen features each split is allowed to consider
The number of trees in the forest
The depth of each tree
questions.answer: How many randomly chosen features each split is allowed to consider
questions.explanation: Limiting the features considered at each split makes trees different from one another, which improves averaging. The number of trees is n_estimators.

questions.q: What does n_estimators set in scikit-learn's RandomForestRegressor?
options: The number of trees in the forest
The number of features checked per split
The maximum depth of each tree
The number of lags created
questions.answer: The number of trees in the forest
questions.explanation: n_estimators is the count of trees whose predictions are averaged. Depth and features per split are separate settings.

questions.q: What are out-of-bag (OOB) observations for a tree in a random forest?
options: Rows with missing values that are dropped before any tree is grown, so they never influence the error estimate
The test set chosen by the analyst
Outliers removed before training
Training rows not selected in that tree's bootstrap sample, which can be used to estimate error
questions.answer: Training rows not selected in that tree's bootstrap sample, which can be used to estimate error
questions.explanation: Each bootstrap sample leaves out some rows, and the tree can be checked on them. They are not the analyst's test set or dropped data.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a random forest over a single decision tree?
options: It is easier to read as a set of rules
It can extrapolate growth trends beyond the highest sales levels seen in the training data
It reduces variance, giving more stable and usually more accurate forecasts
It needs no hyperparameters
questions.answer: It reduces variance, giving more stable and usually more accurate forecasts
questions.explanation: Averaging many decorrelated trees cancels out much of each tree's noise. A forest is less readable than one tree and still cannot extrapolate.

questions.q: Which scikit-learn class fits a random forest for numeric forecasting targets?
options: RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.tree
DecisionTreeRegressor from sklearn.ensemble
RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.ensemble
XGBRegressor from sklearn.ensemble
questions.answer: RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.ensemble
questions.explanation: RandomForestRegressor lives in sklearn.ensemble. DecisionTreeRegressor is in sklearn.tree, and XGBRegressor comes from the separate xgboost library.

questions.q: How is impurity-based feature importance computed in a random forest?
options: As the regression coefficient of the feature
As the average reduction in error (impurity) from splits on that feature, across all trees
As the correlation between the feature and the target, computed on the full training dataset
As the number of missing values in the feature
questions.answer: As the average reduction in error (impurity) from splits on that feature, across all trees
questions.explanation: The forest adds up how much each feature reduced error in each tree and averages over trees. It is not a coefficient or a simple correlation.

questions.q: A random forest with 4 trees forecasts tomorrow's sales at a Mumbai outlet as 480, 520, 500 and 540 units. What is the forest's forecast?
options: 510 units
500 units
540 units
2,040 units
questions.answer: 510 units
questions.explanation: (480 + 520 + 500 + 540)/4 = 2,040/4 = 510. 2,040 is the sum and 540 is just the highest tree.

questions.q: A random forest classifier of 7 trees predicts whether a SKU will stock out next week: 4 trees say 'Stock-out' and 3 say 'No stock-out'. What is the forecast?
options: No stock-out
Undecided, since it is close
Stock-out with probability 0.43
Stock-out
questions.answer: Stock-out
questions.explanation: Classification forests use majority vote, and 4 of 7 is a majority. The share of votes for stock-out is 4/7 = 0.57, not 0.43.

questions.q: For a large training set, roughly what share of rows is left out of each tree's bootstrap sample?
options: About 63%
Exactly 50%
About 10%
About 37%
questions.answer: About 37%
questions.explanation: The chance a row is never drawn is (1 - 1/n)^n, about 0.368. About 63% of distinct rows are included, which is the common mix-up.

questions.q: A random forest for daily sales gives importances: lag_7 = 0.40, lag_1 = 0.30, promo = 0.15, temperature = 0.10, holiday = 0.05. What is the most reasonable business reading?
options: A 1-unit rise in lag_7 raises sales by 0.40 units
Holidays have no real effect on sales and can safely be ignored in all future store-level demand planning
Sales on the same weekday last week is the most useful predictor, pointing to a strong weekly pattern
Promotions cause 15% of sales
questions.answer: Sales on the same weekday last week is the most useful predictor, pointing to a strong weekly pattern
questions.explanation: lag_7 being most important signals weekly seasonality. Importances are not coefficients or causal shares, and a low score does not prove zero effect.

questions.q: Increasing a random forest from 100 to 1,000 trees changes test RMSE from 41.2 to 41.0. What is the best interpretation?
options: The forest is now badly overfitting
The error has stabilised; more trees add computation cost with little benefit
1,000 trees is always required
The forest is now overfitting badly, so the number of trees should be cut back to 100
questions.answer: The error has stabilised; more trees add computation cost with little benefit
questions.explanation: Adding trees reduces variance up to a point and then levels off; it does not usually cause overfitting. The tiny gain here is not worth ten times the computation.

questions.q: In a sales forest, lag_1 is by far the strongest feature. Why does considering only a random subset of features at each split (max_features below 1.0) often help?
options: It stops every tree splitting on lag_1 first, so trees differ and their average is steadier
It removes lag_1 from the model entirely
It makes each individual tree more accurate on its own, so far fewer trees are needed in the forest
It allows the forest to extrapolate trends
questions.answer: It stops every tree splitting on lag_1 first, so trees differ and their average is steadier
questions.explanation: If all trees used the same dominant split they would be highly correlated and averaging would help little. Random feature subsets decorrelate the trees, even though each tree is slightly weaker.

questions.q: A random forest is trained on monthly sales that never exceeded Rs 2 crore. The business expects Rs 2.5 crore next Diwali. What will the forest likely do?
options: Forecast no more than about Rs 2 crore, because it averages leaf values from the training range
Forecast Rs 2.5 crore by extending the trend
Forecast well above Rs 2 crore, because averaging hundreds of trees lets it extend the recent upward trend
Refuse to make a forecast
questions.answer: Forecast no more than about Rs 2 crore, because it averages leaf values from the training range
questions.explanation: Every tree outputs averages of past values, and so does their mean. Forests share the single tree's inability to extrapolate.

questions.q: A forest has training R-squared 0.98 but R-squared 0.62 on the latest 6 months held out. What is a sensible next step?
options: Report the 0.98 as the model's accuracy
Shuffle the data so test R-squared improves
Reduce the number of trees to 1
Constrain the trees (e.g. larger min_samples_leaf or smaller max_depth) and check whether recent months show a trend or shift
questions.answer: Constrain the trees (e.g. larger min_samples_leaf or smaller max_depth) and check whether recent months show a trend or shift
questions.explanation: The gap points to overfitting or a change in the series over time. Regularising the trees and checking for trend addresses it; shuffling would only hide it.

questions.q: A random forest will forecast monthly sales 3 months ahead directly (not recursively). Which lag features can be used?
options: lag_1 and lag_2 only
lag_1 and older lags
lag_3 and older lags
Any lag, including lag_0
questions.answer: lag_3 and older lags
questions.explanation: At forecast time only data up to 3 months before the target month is known, so lag_1 and lag_2 would be future values. Using them causes leakage.

questions.q: After shuffling the 'promo' column in the test set, a forest's RMSE rises from 40 to 70. What does this show?
options: Promo is unimportant, since a feature that matters would leave the RMSE unchanged after shuffling
Promo is an important feature, since breaking its link to sales worsens error by 30
Promo should be shuffled permanently
The model is overfitting on promo
questions.answer: Promo is an important feature, since breaking its link to sales worsens error by 30
questions.explanation: Permutation importance measures how much error increases when a feature's information is destroyed. A large increase means the model relies on that feature.

questions.q: Each tree in a forest has prediction variance 400, the average correlation between trees is 0.3, and there are 100 trees. Using variance = rho x sigma^2 + (1 - rho) x sigma^2 / n, what is the variance of the forest's average?
questions.explanation: 0.3 x 400 + 0.7 x 400 / 100 = 120 + 2.8 = 122.8. 4 assumes independent trees (sigma^2/n), which ignores correlation; 120 is the floor reached only with infinitely many trees.

questions.q: With a training set of 5 rows, what is the probability that a particular row is NOT chosen in a bootstrap sample of size 5 (to 2 decimals)?
questions.explanation: (1 - 1/5)^5 = 0.8^5 = 0.33. 0.80 is the chance of missing on a single draw, and 0.67 is the chance the row is chosen.

questions.q: An online fashion platform's sales grow 25% a year. A random forest on sales levels badly under-forecasts the 2025 festive sale. Which remedy is most appropriate?
options: Add 1,000 more trees
Increase max_depth to reach higher values
Rely on the out-of-bag error instead of a test set, as it already reflects the festive peak in sales
Forecast year-on-year growth or the residual after a trend, then convert back to levels
questions.answer: Forecast year-on-year growth or the residual after a trend, then convert back to levels
questions.explanation: The forest cannot exceed training levels, so the target must be made stationary (growth or detrended) first. More or deeper trees still average past levels.

questions.q: An analyst reports a random forest's out-of-bag (OOB) score of 0.95 as evidence of daily sales forecast accuracy. Why can this be misleading for forecasting?
options: OOB scores are always lower than test scores
OOB is only valid for classification
OOB rows are random days whose neighbouring past and future days were in training, so the score is optimistic; a time-ordered hold-out is needed
OOB uses the same rows as training, so it equals the training score
questions.answer: OOB rows are random days whose neighbouring past and future days were in training, so the score is optimistic; a time-ordered hold-out is needed
questions.explanation: Bootstrap sampling ignores time, so out-of-bag days are surrounded by training days on both sides. True forecasting accuracy must be measured on a later period.

questions.q: A retailer must forecast 2,000 SKUs whose sales depend on price, promotions and weather, with strong interactions. A single stable SKU with no external drivers is also forecast. Which statement is most accurate?
options: SARIMA is always better because it is designed for time series
Random forest is always better because it is machine learning
A random forest suits the driver-rich, interacting SKUs, while a classical model like SARIMA can stay competitive for the single stable series
Both models require the data to be shuffled first
questions.answer: A random forest suits the driver-rich, interacting SKUs, while a classical model like SARIMA can stay competitive for the single stable series
questions.explanation: Forests exploit many external drivers and non-linear interactions; classical models shine on clean univariate series. Model choice should follow the data, not the label.

questions.q: In a forest for store sales, 'store_id' (800 distinct values) shows the highest impurity-based importance, but shuffling it barely changes test error. What is the best explanation?
options: store_id is truly the main driver of sales
Impurity importance is biased toward features with many possible split points; permutation importance is more reliable here
Permutation importance is always wrong for forests
The forest has too few trees
questions.answer: Impurity importance is biased toward features with many possible split points; permutation importance is more reliable here
questions.explanation: High-cardinality and continuous features offer many splits and can inflate impurity importance. Permutation on held-out data shows the real contribution is small.

questions.q: A forest includes both lag_1 and rolling_mean_3 (correlation 0.92). Each shows moderate importance, but dropping both badly hurts accuracy. Why?
options: Correlated features share importance between them, so each looks less important than the information they jointly carry
Both features are useless and dropping them is safe
Forests cannot use correlated features
Importance values must always sum to the R-squared
questions.answer: Correlated features share importance between them, so each looks less important than the information they jointly carry
questions.explanation: When two features carry the same information, trees split on either, so credit is divided. Their combined value only shows when both are removed.

questions.q: Five trees in a forest predict 90, 100, 110, 120 and 130 units. What are the forecast and the standard deviation of the tree predictions (population formula)?
questions.explanation: Mean = 110; squared deviations 400, 100, 0, 100, 400 average 200, so SD = sqrt(200) = 14.1. 200 is the variance and 40 is the range.

questions.q: An analyst creates rolling_mean_7 for daily sales using a centred 7-day window (3 days before, the day itself, 3 days after) and the forest's test error is suspiciously low. What is the fix?
options: Use a 30-day centred window instead
Add more trees to the forest
Drop the time-ordered split
Compute the rolling mean only from past days, shifted so it excludes the day being forecast
questions.answer: Compute the rolling mean only from past days, shifted so it excludes the day being forecast
questions.explanation: A centred window includes the target and future days, which are unknown at forecast time. Shifting the window to past days only removes the leakage.

questions.q: A small analytics team with little tuning time needs a robust first machine learning model for weekly demand. Why is a random forest often a good first choice over XGBoost?
options: Random forests always beat XGBoost in accuracy
Random forests can extrapolate trends and XGBoost cannot
Random forests perform well with default settings and are less prone to overfitting when lightly tuned
XGBoost cannot use lag features
questions.answer: Random forests perform well with default settings and are less prone to overfitting when lightly tuned
questions.explanation: Forests are forgiving of hyperparameters, while boosting usually needs careful tuning of learning rate, depth and rounds. Neither extrapolates trends, and both use lag features.

references: A random forest is a collection of many decision trees whose forecasts are averaged. Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the data, drawn with replacement, and at each split it only considers a random subset of features. This makes the trees different from one another, so their individual errors partly cancel out when averaged, giving a more stable and accurate forecast than a single tree. For forecasting we feed it lag, rolling and calendar features, tune settings like number of trees and leaf size on a later validation period, read feature importance carefully, and remember it cannot forecast beyond past levels.

Say a retail chain wants tomorrow's sales for each store. One decision tree might say 480, but it is jumpy. A random forest builds, say, 500 trees, each on a slightly different random sample of days and features like last week's sales, promotions, weekday and festivals. The trees forecast 480, 520, 500, 540 and so on, and we take the average. Feature importance then shows that last week's same-day sales matter most, pointing to a weekly pattern. We test it on the latest weeks, not on random or out-of-bag days, and handle growth trends separately because averages of trees cannot exceed history.

As a manager I see random forest as a robust, low-maintenance machine learning workhorse. It captures non-linear effects and interactions between drivers like price, promotion and weather, resists overfitting thanks to bagging and random feature selection, and works well with default settings. The trade-offs: it is less transparent than one tree, slower with many trees, cannot extrapolate trends, and its importance scores can mislead with correlated or high-cardinality features. I would use it when there are many drivers and SKUs, insist on a time-ordered test, check for leakage in rolling features, and compare it against SARIMA or Holt-Winters before trusting it.

questions.q: How does gradient boosting build its trees?
options: Sequentially, with each new tree trying to correct the errors of the trees before it
Independently and in parallel on bootstrap samples, with their forecasts then averaged together
As one very deep tree
By randomly deleting trees from a forest
questions.answer: Sequentially, with each new tree trying to correct the errors of the trees before it
questions.explanation: Boosting adds trees one after another, each focused on what the current model gets wrong. Independent, parallel trees describe random forests.

questions.q: With squared-error loss, what does each new tree in gradient boosting learn to predict?
options: The original target values
The feature importances
The average of all previous trees
The residuals (errors) of the current model
questions.answer: The residuals (errors) of the current model
questions.explanation: For squared error the negative gradient equals the residual, so each tree models what is left unexplained. Predicting the raw target again would ignore earlier trees.

questions.q: What does the learning_rate (eta) parameter do in XGBoost?
options: It sets the number of trees
It sets the depth of each tree
It scales down each new tree's contribution to the forecast
It sets the share of the most recent data held back for validation and testing
questions.answer: It scales down each new tree's contribution to the forecast
questions.explanation: Each tree's output is multiplied by the learning rate before being added, so smaller values make learning slower but more careful.

questions.q: What does XGBoost stand for?
options: Extra Generalised Bagging
eXtreme Gradient Boosting
Exponential Gradient Bootstrapping
Extended Gini Boosting
questions.answer: eXtreme Gradient Boosting
questions.explanation: XGBoost is an optimised, regularised implementation of gradient boosting. It is not a bagging method.

questions.q: What do XGBoost's reg_lambda and reg_alpha parameters do?
options: They set the learning rate
They penalise large leaf weights to reduce overfitting
They choose which lags to create
They control how many of the most recent rows are kept aside as the test set
questions.answer: They penalise large leaf weights to reduce overfitting
questions.explanation: Lambda (L2) and alpha (L1) shrink leaf values, making the model more conservative. This built-in regularisation is a key difference from basic gradient boosting.

questions.q: What is early stopping in XGBoost?
options: Stopping the addition of trees when validation error has not improved for a set number of rounds
Stopping training after the first tree
Removing trees that have low importance
Ending training as soon as the training error stops falling or reaches zero on the full training dataset
